_: No explicit regulations or bans on cryptocurrencies. RBI's previous banking ban was reversed by the Supreme Court in 2020.
All buying, selling, transactions, and mining of cryptocurrencies are illegal as of 2021.
Bitcoin classified as a convertible decentralized virtual currency by the U.S. Treasury. CFTC classified as a commodity. IRS taxes as property.
Banned as a payment instrument, but still allowed to be traded. Banned for use in banking transactions.
No specific regulation on cryptocurrencies yet.
The Central Bank of Nigeria banned bank transactions in bitcoin and other virtual currencies in 2017 and reaffirmed the ban in 2021.
No regulations against cryptocurrencies. Proposed legislation in 2020 for business use regulations.
Not a method of payment domestically but legally recognized. Legal to trade, though warnings about volatility exist.
Bitcoin legal since 2017. Plans to regulate it as a virtual asset under the FinTech Law.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal. Japanese regulators have a hands-off approach, allowing digital assets to prosper.
Egypt's Dar al-Ifta has issued a religious decree classifying commercial transactions in bitcoin as haram (prohibited under Islamic law).
Legal to hold and trade cryptocurrencies, with risks explained by the central bank.
The government has not banned the trading or holding of cryptocurrencies.
Legal to hold cryptocurrencies but banned in banking transactions.
Legal in Germany. Treated as private money for tax purposes. Not considered legal tender or foreign currency.
Not officially banned, but advised against by the Bank of Tanzania.
Legal to trade and hold bitcoin. Ban lifted in 2014.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies. No regulatory legislation prohibiting their use.
Legal to trade and hold bitcoin. Government is supportive of cryptocurrency development.
No legal status or regulatory framework for virtual currencies, classified as intangible assets for tax purposes.
Legal to hold and trade cryptocurrencies. No specific legislation regarding taxation of cryptocurrency income.
Legal to use but banks prohibited from dealing with cryptocurrencies.
Legal to buy, sell, and trade cryptocurrencies.
The purchase, sale, use, and holding of virtual currency is prohibited. Any breach is punishable.
Legal to trade and hold bitcoin. Cryptocurrencies are not considered financial instruments under Spanish law.
Cryptocurrencies not prohibited. Tax laws include profits from digital currencies as taxable income.
Banned for use in banking transactions. Bitcoin-related business models regulated in Quebec. BMO and TD banned cryptocurrency purchases with their cards.
No legislation against Bitcoin, though government advises against its use.
Legal framework for the cryptocurrency industry established in March 2022. Crypto donations raised over $63.8 million during the Russian invasion.
Explicit ban on cryptocurrencies, with penalties for transactions.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to hold and trade. PIT-38 form for cryptocurrency taxes released in 2020.
Legal to trade but not legal tender. Central Bank does not regulate Bitcoin.
Legal to trade, but banking institutions prohibited from dealing with crypto unless approved.
Since 2017, the Nepal Rastra Bank has maintained that all transactions related to or regarding bitcoins are illegal.
Cryptocurrencies and mining are legal in Venezuela, amidst hyperinflation.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies. Licensing framework for exchanges is under development.
Legal to trade, but increased regulation and warnings from financial authorities. Banned for use in banking transactions.
One of the top bitcoin mining countries. 15% tax on cryptocurrency income.
No regulations prohibiting cryptocurrencies. Proposal in 2021 for recognizing and regulating them as a legal means of payment.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to hold and trade. Considered digital assets or commodities, not legal tender.
Legal to trade and hold bitcoin. No regulations prohibiting cryptocurrencies.
Central Bank states that buying/selling crypto is not forbidden but not an authorized payment method.
Cryptocurrencies legal to trade but banned for use in banking transactions.
The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe is skeptical but BitMari received a license in 2017 to operate.
Legal to trade and hold bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. Warnings about risks associated with their use.
The Central Bank of Jordan prohibits banks, currency exchange companies, and financial entities from facilitating cryptocurrency transactions.
Legal to trade cryptocurrencies, with regulations for licensing by the Securities and Commodities Authority.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies, classified as property. No legislation against trading or mining.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are considered commodities. They are legal to trade and own. Czech banks can offer cryptocurrency-related services if AML/KYC regulations
Cryptocurrency tax haven with 0% tax on bitcoin-derived income.
Legal to hold and trade cryptocurrencies. No explicit regulatory legislation on taxation of cryptocurrency income.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are taxable assets. A 25% capital gains tax applies to sales, with miners and traders subject to corporate income tax and VAT.
No laws specifically prohibiting or regulating bitcoin.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to hold and trade. Austrian law does not explicitly prohibit cryptocurrencies.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to hold and trade. Zug is known as "Crypto Valley." Plans to make bitcoin legal tender in Lugano, announced in 2022.
Cryptocurrency transactions legalized under Decree No. 8 in March 2018.
Bitcoin is considered a commodity. It is legally mined, bought, sold, and traded on local exchanges.
Bitcoins are being used in the country.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to trade and hold. The sale of virtual currencies is subject to income tax.
Bitcoin was made legal tender in 2021 through the "Bitcoin Law."
Legal to buy, sell, and hold cryptocurrencies. No regulation from the Financial Supervisory Authority.
Both trading and holding of bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are allowed. A popular location for crypto companies due to favorable regulation.
Despite warnings from the Lebanese Central Bank, laws do not prohibit the ownership, use, and trade of Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies.
Bitcoin became legal tender on April 27, 2022.
Bitcoin is recognized as an asset and legal to trade and hold. Taxed at a fixed 15% rate.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies. Taxed as private contracts for difference.
No laws specifically prohibiting or regulating bitcoin. Guidance provided in 2018 that cryptocurrency revenues must be taxed.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies. No blanket prohibition.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to trade and hold. No specific regulations but contract and tax laws apply.
Not considered legal tender, but not illegal. A few merchants accept bitcoins.
No regulations prohibiting cryptocurrencies. Proposals introduced for regulation and legal certainty.
Legal to hold and trade bitcoin. Cryptocurrencies are not considered a legal means of payment.
Income tax exemption on profits from crypto sales and no legislative restrictions. Georgia is a hub for bitcoin miners.
Qatar's central bank announced that it is illegal to trade bitcoin in the country.
Cryptocurrency exchanges are not allowed, and cryptocurrency cannot be accepted as payment for goods or services.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to trade and hold. No plans to limit transactions in virtual currencies.
Not explicitly prohibited, but cryptocurrencies are not legal tender in Jamaica.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are legal to trade and hold. Income is taxed at a fixed 15% personal income tax rate.
Regulated by Law No. 66/2020 "On Financial Markets based on Distributed Registry Technology," licensing entities in cryptocurrency distribution and trading.
No laws specifically prohibiting or regulating bitcoin. FURS provided guidelines on taxation for cryptocurrencies in 2017.
Trading and use of Bitcoin is illegal.
Legal for citizens to buy, store, and sell cryptocurrencies. Not recognized as legal tender.
Not illegal but not regulated. Businesses enjoy relaxed regulation.
Legal to trade and hold cryptocurrencies. Draft legislation for tighter regulations introduced in 2022.
Regulated as Digital Assets under the Financial Services Act. Caution for investors due to lack of statutory protections.
Legal to trade and hold. Regulated with tax guidelines for digital assets, dubbed "The Blockchain Island".
Bitcoin and cryptocurrency are legal to hold and trade but not regulated by AMBD.
Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are not considered legal tender, but not illegal to trade. Iceland is home to large bitcoin mining facilities due to low energy costs.
Legal to trade and hold / Illegal as payment
Legal to trade and hold / Illegal as payment
Legal / Illegal as a payment tool, banking ban
Legal to trade and hold / Illegal as payment
Legal / Illegal to buy with local currency
Legal to hold / Illegal to mine
Legal to trade/hold / Illegal as payment tool, banking ban
Not recognized as legal tender but not banned. Regulatory uncertainty remains.
Financial institutions cannot facilitate bitcoin transactions. Cryptocurrency exchanges and mining were fully banned on 24 September 2021.
Bitcoin is classified as a virtual currency, a commodity, and taxable property. Crypto businesses must follow AML regulations.

Cryptocurrencies are banned as payment tools since 1 January 2018. A 2021 fatwa declared cryptocurrency haram unless meeting Islamic trade criteria. In 2022, cryptocurrencies were classified as "monitored financial technologies."
Not regulated, but arrests have occurred for mining and money laundering concerns
Banks are prohibited from facilitating cryptocurrency transactions. However, the government is exploring blockchain adoption. Violations attract penalties.
A licensing regime for crypto service providers was established in December 2022. Crypto was previously discouraged due to operational risks.
Crypto transactions criminalized under anti-money laundering laws.

Cryptocurrency is considered a monetary substitute by Russian law, with mining legal but a banking ban on crypto-related transactions. In 2021, Russia accepted cryptocurrencies for international trade. However, domestic cryptocurrency payments remain banned.
Bitcoin is legal, with plans to regulate it as a virtual asset under the FinTech Law.
Bitcoin is not considered currency but can be used for transactions. Since April 2017, cryptocurrency exchanges must register and comply with security and anti-money laundering regulations.
Individuals, banks, and financial institutions are prohibited from dealing in cryptocurrencies.
Cryptocurrency exchanges are regulated by the Central Bank under Circular 944. Bitcoin is not considered legal currency.
The use of bitcoin as payment is illegal and subject to fines, but trading it as a virtual asset is allowed.
Banks prohibited from facilitating crypto transactions.
Banned for payments in 2021 due to transaction risks.
Bitcoin is considered "private money" and is taxed like euro transactions. Banks can sell and store cryptocurrencies since 2020.
The Bank of Tanzania advises against cryptocurrency use, emphasizing that the Tanzanian shilling is the only legal tender.

Cryptocurrency trading is allowed but must be in Thai Baht. From 1 April 2022, using cryptocurrencies for payments is prohibited. Commercial banks are cautioned against direct involvement in digital assets.
As of 2013, bitcoin is unregulated in the UK and treated as foreign currency for most purposes. VAT is due on goods/services exchanged for bitcoin. Profits/losses are subject to capital gains tax.
In July 2014, the French Ministry of Finance issued regulations concerning virtual currency professionals, exchanges, and taxation.
The Reserve Bank declared virtual currency has no legal status or regulatory framework. The South African Revenue Service classifies bitcoin as an intangible asset.
Italy does not regulate bitcoin use by private individuals.
Financial institutions cannot facilitate bitcoin transactions. The Superintendencia Financiera prohibited banks from engaging with virtual currencies in 2014.
Minors and foreigners cannot trade cryptocurrencies. South Korean adults can trade using real-name accounts at banks. Both banks and exchanges enforce anti-money laundering measures.
The purchase, sale, use, and holding of virtual currency are prohibited. Violations are punishable under existing laws.
Bitcoin transactions are subject to the same laws as barter transactions.
Bitcoin is considered a "good" under civil law but not legal currency. In May 2022, the Central Bank banned financial institutions from facilitating crypto transactions.
Taliban banned crypto trading in August 2022.
Crypto companies must register with FINTRAC and comply with AML laws. Some banks restrict crypto purchases.
Government officials have advised against bitcoin use, but there is no legislation prohibiting it.
Ukraine legalized cryptocurrency in March 2022 but banned purchasing it with local currency, allowing purchases only with foreign currencies under a $3300 limit.
Transactions via virtual currencies violate exchange regulations. Authorities warn of risks like money laundering and terrorist financing
Bitcoin is not considered legal tender, but it is not illegal. Some risks are associated with it, as noted by financial authorities.
Crypto trading and mining legalized in 2018; tax-free.
Bitcoin is not legal tender but is not regulated. In 2024, authorities allowed cryptocurrency to be used for zakat payments with a 2.5% rate.
Financial institutions warned against using bitcoin.
Bitcoin ownership is legal. However, in March 2023, authorities banned cryptocurrency mining due to corruption concerns, and the ban remained in place as of June.

In December 2013, the Reserve Bank of Australia stated there’s no law against using competing currencies like bitcoin. From April 2018, exchanges must register with the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre.
Financial institutions cannot facilitate bitcoin transactions. Regulators warn bitcoin has no legal protection. Bitcoin ATMs are not allowed.
There are no regulations on bitcoin usage.
Bitcoin use is regulated under Law 210/2019, with income from trading classified as "income from other sources."
As of 2013, bitcoin is not classified as money in the Netherlands. Cryptocurrencies must be declared, and taxes must be paid.
Cryptocurrencies cannot be used as a payment tool, but buying and selling them is legal. Banks strictly block crypto-related transactions.
The National Bank of Cambodia prohibits banks from allowing cryptocurrency transactions.
The Reserve Bank banned crypto banking, but a High Court Order lifted the ban. The matter remains unresolved.
The Central Bank banned bitcoin and all unregulated digital currencies in 2014. A 2020 resolution repealed the original ban.
In July 2013, the Minister of Finance expressed concerns over Bitcoin's use for money laundering but did not see a need for government intervention.
Central Bank prohibits financial institutions from dealing in crypto. Some merchants still accept it.
Central Bank does not recognize crypto for payments yet. Regulations exist for crypto assets.
The Swedish Tax Agency ruled that bitcoin transactions are not subject to VAT but are treated as currency by the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, with applicable regulations for businesses.
Businesses dealing in cryptocurrencies must comply with anti-money laundering laws
In 2013, the Bank of Portugal warned that Bitcoin was not a safe currency. By 2014, there was no specific legal framework for Bitcoin.
No specific legislation on bitcoins exists in Greece.
Treated as a taxable asset with capital gains tax.
The Hungarian Central Bank issued warnings but did not make cryptocurrencies illegal.
Cryptocurrencies are not official currency but are subject to tax law. The Financial Market Authority warns investors about risks.
Bitcoin businesses are subject to anti-money laundering regulations. No legislative action is required currently.

The Decree On the Development of Digital Economy allows residents to engage in cryptocurrency operations, including mining, token creation, and exchange services, with exemptions on revenue and profits from operations with tokens until 2023.
Bitcoin is considered a commodity but restricted in domestic settlements.

Bitcoin is considered a virtual commodity. No direct legislation but monitored under anti-money laundering laws. A regulatory framework was finalized in 2023, and new Virtual Asset Trading Platform regulations took effect in mid-2024.
The government had not issued regulations or guidance on Bitcoin as of 2014. An American banker used bitcoin to purchase real estate.
No specific mention of bitcoin in Bulgarian laws. Individuals must pay 10% tax on profits from trading.
Bitcoin became legal tender on 7 September 2021. While 12% of consumers used it in the first month, 93% of businesses reported receiving no bitcoin payments.

Denmark's Financial Supervisory Authority (FSA) declared bitcoin is not a currency and does not regulate its use. In 2017, FSA stated that doing business with bitcoin does not fall under its regulatory authority.

Businesses can choose whether to accept bitcoin. The Monetary Authority of Singapore warns of risks but does not intervene. Bitcoin is classified as a digital payment token under the Payment Services Act.
Bitcoin was declared legal tender in April 2022 but repealed in April 2023.

The Norwegian Tax Administration treats bitcoin as an asset, subjecting profits to wealth tax. Bitcoin transactions in business fall under sales tax regulations, but the government exempted VAT on the purchase or sale of bitcoin.

The Finnish Tax Administration considers bitcoin transactions as private contracts for tax purposes. Bitcoin is taxable on its increase in value, but losses are not tax-deductible. Mined bitcoin is considered earned income.
Bitcoin is not classified as currency and is not regulated. Risks are associated with participation in virtual currency activities.
The Central Bank of Ireland stated in December 2013 that it does not regulate bitcoin, and bitcoin is not legal tender in the EU.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand stated that non-banks don't need approval for bitcoin schemes that don't involve issuing physical currency.
The Central Bank stated in 2017 that cryptocurrencies are not considered legal currency and cannot be traded on the national payment system. Users assume all risks.
Financial authorities warn about digital wallet theft and fraud. No direct regulation.
Based on a public decision in 2019, crypto income is not considered "Georgian sourced," and it falls under a 0% tax on capital gains derived from crypto trading.
Banks cannot trade crypto; banned in Qatar Financial Centre.
Cryptocurrency exchanges are not allowed, and crypto cannot be used for payments.
No regulation on the use of bitcoins.
The Bank of Jamaica supports exploring cryptocurrency technology and launched a campaign to raise awareness in 2017.
The Bank of Lithuania warned that bitcoin is not recognized as legal tender, advising users about the high risks associated with using it.
On 21 May 2020, Albania passed a new law to regulate cryptocurrency activities.
Bitcoin is not considered currency or asset, but businesses selling goods/services in bitcoin are taxed.
No specific legislation on bitcoins or cryptocurrency exists. However, the National Bank warned against scams like ONECOIN.
The Central Bank is open to working with fintech and crypto firms but warns of risks, criminal use, and lack of insurance or regulatory protections.
The use of bitcoin is not regulated in Cyprus.
In Estonia, the use of bitcoins is not regulated or controlled by the government, and there are no legal obstacles to using bitcoin-like cryptocurrencies for payments.
Cryptocurrencies are regulated as Digital Assets under the Financial Services Act 2007, but investors are not protected by statutory compensation agreements.
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka supported cryptocurrencies and planned to make bitcoin legal tender by 2023.
In February 2014, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier acknowledged bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as currency. The first BitLicence was issued in 2015.
As of 2017, no specific regulations on bitcoins. The prime minister announced a national strategy to promote bitcoin and blockchain technology.
Bitcoin is not legal tender and not regulated. Authorities warn against investment scams but do not prohibit trading or holding.

Iceland restricts foreign exchange trading with bitcoin but allows bitcoin mining. In 2017, the Central Bank granted exemptions to previous rules, providing more flexibility for virtual currency transactions.
The use of cryptocurrencies in Samoa is legal but discouraged by the Central Bank of Samoa.
Tonga plans to make bitcoin legal tender by the end of 2023. This has been planned since late 2021.
Gibraltar introduced a regulatory framework in 2018 for businesses using distributed ledger technology.
Decentralised autonomous organisations (DAOs), which are blockchain-based, are considered legal entities in the Marshall Islands.
The use of cryptocurrencies is officially supported by the government.
The government officially supports the use of blockchain technologies, including cryptocurrencies.
